paras: The lynching of John Baker was the reported hanging of a farm hand by his fellow threshing workers on the farm of a man named Weeks near Guide Rock, in Webster County, Nebraska, on September 1, 1888. Baker was accused of feeding the boy who cut bands on the crew into the threshing machine after the boy accidentally cut his hand, and the other hands hanged him from the machine's straw carrier. The story ran nationally under an "Agenda, Kan." dateline, and one Kansas editor called it a fabrication that had fooled the Associated Press.

The wire dispatch described Guide Rock as "a small town just over the Nebraska line" from Agenda, Kansas, where the report was dated. A special from Guide Rock to the Omaha Bee noted that Webster County had seen the lynching of "the desperado Bill Cole" about two weeks earlier, and the McCook Tribune ran the new report as the county's second lynching in ten days. According to that account, Weeks was having his threshing done, with Baker feeding the thresher and a young boy cutting bands for him.

While the men were at work, the boy's knife slipped as he cut a band and struck Baker on the hand, leaving "an ugly wound." The Omaha Bee account said Baker seized the boy, threw him on the platform and pushed him feet first into the thresher "as if he were a sheaf of grain." By the time the other men heard the boy's screams over the noise of the machine, half of his body had disappeared, and he was dead.

Baker jumped from the platform and tried to escape, but the men caught him. One of them shouted "Hang him!", a rope was put around Baker's neck, and a man climbed onto the straw carrier to pass it through an iron rod. With his arms pinioned, Baker was hauled up by "a half dozen strong hands" while the platform was still covered with the boy's blood. Shorter items said he was lynched "promptly" or "on the spot"; an Idaho brief said "that night."
None of the reports gives the boy's name, and no report of an inquest, arrest or legal action against the men who hanged Baker appears in the coverage.

The wire version, datelined Agenda, Kansas, September 2, appeared on September 3 in dailies from Maine to California, among them the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Daily Kennebec Journal, the New York Sun and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. Its headlines dwelt on the boy's death: the Kennebec Journal ran "Fiendish Fury," and the Globe told of an "Enragged Feeder" who was "Hanged to the Straw Carrier by the Other Hands." Shortened versions ran through mid-September, including in the Emporia Weekly News and the Atlanta Constitution. Condensing blurred the place: the Portland Daily Press and the Republican Journal set the event "near Angenda" or "Augenda, Kansas," the Iowa Plain Dealer put Guide Rock in Kansas, and the Maysville Evening Bulletin called Baker "a Nebraska farmer."

The Turner County Herald headed its item "Quick Justice" and wrote that Baker "perished while his hands were yet wet with the life blood of his victim." The Kansas City Indicator, as quoted in the Barbour County Index, called Baker a "fiend in human shape" who was "justly lynched." The Omaha Bee special, by contrast, called the hanging an "outbreak of lawless justice," though it described it as the sequel to one of the most horrible crimes on record. No paper stated the race of Baker, the boy or the men who hanged him.

Accounts differed on place and date: the local special named Webster County, Nebraska, and Saturday the 1st, while some condensed items moved the event to Kansas and the Sturgis Advertiser said "Monday last."

On September 12 the Barbour County Index of Medicine Lodge, Kansas, said the same item had been offered to it four weeks earlier as an affair in Harper County, Kansas. The Index said it had refused the item and later saw that the Associated Press had been "gulled" into publishing it. No other paper repeated that claim, and the Guide Rock special supplied details not found in the wire version.

reader.title: Lynching of John Baker
bases: Fellow threshing hands seized John Baker after he was accused of killing a boy and hanged him from the machine's straw carrier (A2, A33, A24).

As reported, a group of farm hands, 'a half dozen strong hands' on the rope, hanged Baker without any legal process as punishment for killing the boy, which papers called 'Quick Justice' and 'lawless justice' (A33, A24, A19); the Barbour County Index claimed the story was a fabrication that fooled the Associated Press (A31), so the occurrence itself is disputed.

A wire dispatch and an independent Guide Rock special to the Omaha Bee agree on the core event (A2, A33, A24), but the Barbour County Index said the item had earlier been offered to it as a Harper County affair and called it a hoax (A31).

framing.detail: Dailies ran the dispatch as 'A horrible affair' under headlines such as 'Fiendish Fury' and 'An Enragged Feeder Puts a Boy Into a Thresher'.
The Turner County Herald headed it 'Quick Justice'; the Kansas City Indicator, quoted by the Index, said Baker was 'justly lynched'.
The Omaha Bee special called it an 'outbreak of lawless justice' but the sequel to one of the most horrible crimes on record.
The Barbour County Index reprinted the story only to say it was false and had deceived the Associated Press.
